title: The whole human condition
hook: every person carries the whole form of the human condition (Essays 3.2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kidney stone, and your line was patient with pain. Did you let something ache without starting a second fight? A new week starts now. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

Montaigne opens an essay in book three with a strange kind of apology. Other writers, he says, try to shape a human being, to show what a person ought to be. He only describes one. A particular one. And not a very well made one, either: himself. If he could make that man over, he says, he'd make him quite different, but it's done now. Which raises a fair question. Why should anyone read page after page about one ordinary man with his faults and his kidney stone? His answer is a single sentence, and it's today's word.
screen: `OTHERS SHAPE A PERSON.` → `HE ONLY DESCRIBES ONE.` → `WHY READ ABOUT HIM?`

segments.voice: First, the passing. Montaigne says he doesn't paint being, he paints passing. Not a fixed portrait, but a man changing from day to day, even from minute to minute. If he contradicts himself, he says, that's because he's describing a moving thing honestly. Second, the sentence. Every person, he writes, carries the whole form of the human condition. Not a slice of it. The whole. A farmer, a king, a man with a stone in his side: each one holds the full shape of being human, its fears and appetites and kindness and death. So a plain, private life is not too small to study. It's a complete specimen. Third, two ways to hear it. Some readers hear humility: I am no exception, nothing in me is foreign to anyone else. Others hear dignity: nobody is a rough draft of a person, nobody is only a part. Montaigne seems to mean both. He studies himself not because he's special but because he isn't. Fourth, the stranger. At the pharmacy counter, the person ahead of you is easy to see as a back, a delay, a type. Montaigne's sentence won't allow it. That stranger carries the whole of it too: a childhood, a worry about money, a joke they tell well, a body that will one day stop. You don't have to know their story. You only have to remember it's a whole one.
screen: `HE PAINTS PASSING, NOT BEING.` · `EACH PERSON CARRIES THE WHOLE FORM.` · `HUMILITY AND DIGNITY.` · `THE STRANGER IS WHOLE TOO.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE HUMAN CONDITION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see the whole of it in one stranger. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind someone you saw recently and didn't know: a driver, a cashier, a person on the next bench. Hold their face for a moment. Then, quietly, let the rest come in: they were a child once, they have someone they worry about, something makes them laugh, something keeps them up at night. Don't invent a story. Just let them be whole. Breathe with that for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The whole human condition. Montaigne's claim that every person, however ordinary, carries all of it. Today's word.
Your line: the whole of it. Today, pick one stranger, and say the line to yourself as they pass: the whole of it, in them too. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that each person carries the whole form of the human condition as the reason his self-portrait speaks to strangers.

fork.setup: you want to understand human beings. Montaigne has a method. which is it?
options: study one ordinary life closely: his own.
survey as many people as possible.
fork.reveal: he studies himself, not because he's special but because every person carries the whole form of the human condition.

original.script: la forme entière de l'humaine condition

original.note: Montaigne's French: the whole form of the human condition, from Essays 3.2.

trapdoor: what you thought: the human condition is a grand phrase for philosophers.
what it means: every ordinary person carries all of being human, so one life is worth studying.
what a scholar hears: Montaigne pairs it with painting passing, not being: a self that is whole and always changing.
